quiz.explain: It stores energy as height.

lessons.title: Batteries
lessons.summary: Chemistry, capacity and how to make them last.

cards.title: How a battery works
cards.text: A battery has two electrodes separated by an electrolyte. A chemical reaction pushes electrons out of one electrode, through your circuit, and back into the other. Recharging reverses the reaction.

deep.x: A battery converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Two electrodes with different chemical potential are separated by an electrolyte that lets ions move but not electrons.

steps: Chemical reaction at anode releases electrons

deep.x: In a lithium-ion cell

items.b: lithium ions move from anode (graphite) to cathode
charger pushes them back to the anode
thin porous film keeping electrodes apart

deep.x: History
Primary vs secondary
A battery is a controlled chemical reaction that pushes electrons through your circuit.

cards.title: Capacity: Ah and Wh
cards.text: Amp-hours (Ah) say how much charge a battery holds. Multiply by voltage to get energy in watt-hours (Wh), which is what really matters for comparing batteries.

deep.x: Battery capacity is quoted in amp-hours (Ah) or milliamp-hours (mAh), but energy in watt-hours (Wh) is the fair way to compare batteries of different voltages.
Examples
Power banks
A 10,000 mAh power bank stores about 37 Wh at 3.7 V. After conversion losses, it can deliver roughly 60–70% of that to a phone.
Airline rules
Airlines generally allow power banks up to 100 Wh in cabin baggage without approval, and between 100 and 160 Wh with airline approval. They're banned from checked bags.
Compare batteries in watt-hours, not milliamp-hours.

cards.title: Battery chemistries
cards.text: Lead-acid is cheap and heavy (car starter batteries). Lithium-ion packs far more energy per kilo (phones, laptops, EVs). LFP, a lithium iron phosphate variant, trades a little energy density for safety and long life.

deep.x: Different battery chemistries trade energy density, cost, safety and lifespan.
Common types

items.b: safe, long-life, storage and many EVs

deep.x: LFP's rise
Lithium iron phosphate cells contain no cobalt or nickel, are cheaper and tolerate more cycles. They now power a large share of EVs, especially in China, and most home batteries.
New chemistries
The best chemistry depends on whether you need energy, cost, safety or life.

cards.title: C-rate
cards.text: The C-rate compares charge or discharge current with capacity. 1C fully charges or empties a battery in about an hour; 0.5C in two hours; 3C in 20 minutes. High C-rates create heat and wear.

deep.x: The C-rate expresses charge or discharge current relative to capacity. It shows how hard a battery is being worked.
Examples

x: about 1 hour to charge or discharge

deep.x: Why it matters
Charging curve
Fast charging slows down above about 80%, because the cell's voltage rises and the charger reduces current to protect it. That's why EV charging stops are often 10–80%.
High C-rates are fast but hard on batteries.

cards.title: State of charge and cycles
cards.text: Lithium batteries last longer if kept away from 0% and 100% for long periods. Many EVs recommend charging to 80% for daily use and 100% only before long trips.

deep.x: Lithium-ion batteries age faster when kept at very high or very low charge for long periods, especially when warm.
Practical advice

x: For daily use, charging to about 80% extends life
Charge to 100% before long trips, then drive soon after
Avoid leaving devices fully charged in hot cars or sun

deep.x: Phone features
Many phones offer "optimised charging", pausing at 80% overnight and finishing just before you wake.
LFP is different
LFP batteries tolerate 100% charge better, and some manufacturers recommend charging them fully regularly so the battery management system can calibrate.
Middle charge, moderate temperature: that's where lithium is happiest.

cards.title: Why batteries age
cards.text: Each cycle causes tiny chemical changes that slowly reduce capacity. Heat speeds this up a lot. High charge levels and very fast charging add stress too.

deep.x: Every charge and discharge causes tiny, irreversible chemical changes that slowly reduce capacity and increase internal resistance.
Main stress factors
Calendar vs cycle ageing

items: worse with deep cycles and fast charging

deep.x: End of life
A battery is usually considered "worn out" at 70–80% of original capacity. EV batteries at that point can find a second life in stationary storage.
Heat is a battery's worst enemy.

cards.title: Cycle life
cards.text: LFP cells can often manage several thousand full cycles before falling to 80% capacity, which is why they're popular for home storage. Typical NMC cells manage fewer, but store more energy per kilo.

deep.x: Cycle life is the number of full charge-discharge cycles before capacity falls to a threshold, often 80%.
What it means for EVs
Partial cycles
Two charges from 50% to 100% count roughly as one full cycle. Shallow cycles are gentler than deep ones.
Real-world data
Studies of real EV fleets show many batteries keep around 90% of capacity after 100,000–200,000 km, better than many early predictions.
For home storage cycling every day, LFP's long life is a big advantage.

cards.title: Battery management systems
cards.text: A BMS watches every cell's voltage and temperature, balances them, limits current and disconnects the pack if anything goes wrong. Lithium packs must never be used without one.

deep.x: A battery management system (BMS) monitors and protects every cell in a lithium pack. Large lithium packs should never run without one.
Cell balancing
Cells in a pack drift apart slightly. The BMS balances them so no cell is overcharged or over-discharged while others are still mid-range.
State of charge
The BMS estimates remaining charge from voltage, current and temperature. That's the percentage on your phone or EV dashboard.
Protection
The BMS is the battery's brain and bodyguard.

cards.title: Thermal runaway
cards.text: If a lithium cell is damaged, overcharged or overheated, it can start a self-heating reaction that spreads to neighbouring cells. Such fires are hard to extinguish and can reignite.

deep.x: Thermal runaway is a self-heating chain reaction in a lithium cell. Once started, it releases heat and flammable gases and can spread to neighbouring cells.
Causes
Why fires are hard
Burning cells produce their own oxygen from the cathode, so smothering doesn't work well. EV fires need large amounts of water for cooling and can reignite hours or days later.
LFP is safer
Warning signs
A swollen battery is a warning: stop using it and dispose of it safely.

cards.title: Series and parallel packs
cards.text: Cells in series add voltage; cells in parallel add capacity. An EV pack might combine about 100 groups in series to reach roughly 400 V.

deep.x: Battery packs combine cells in series to raise voltage and in parallel to raise capacity and current.
Notation

items.b: four cells in series, about 14.8 V

deep.x: EV voltages
Most EVs use around 400 V packs. Some newer cars use 800 V architectures, allowing faster charging with lower current and thinner cables.
Weakest link
In series, the weakest cell limits the whole string, which is why matched cells and good balancing matter.
Series for voltage, parallel for capacity.

quiz.q: A 12 V, 50 Ah battery stores about…
Charging at 0.5C takes roughly…
What speeds up battery ageing the most?
quiz.explain: Heat and high states of charge add stress.

lessons.title: Solar power
lessons.summary: How panels turn sunlight into electricity.

cards.title: The photovoltaic effect
cards.text: A solar cell is a thin slice of silicon with two differently treated layers. Light knocks electrons loose, and the junction between the layers pushes them in one direction: a DC current.

deep.x: A solar cell turns light directly into electricity. Photons knock electrons loose in silicon, and a built-in electric field at the junction pushes them in one direction.
The junction

items.b: built-in field pushes electrons one way

deep.x: History

events.l: Bell Labs' first practical silicon cell

deep.x: Efficiency
Einstein's 1921 Nobel Prize was awarded for explaining the photoelectric effect, a related phenomenon, not for relativity.

cards.title: Cells, panels, strings
cards.text: A cell makes about 0.5–0.6 V. Dozens of cells in series make a panel; several panels in series make a string with a few hundred volts, feeding an inverter.

deep.x: Solar cells are combined into panels, and panels into strings, to reach useful voltages and powers.
Typical values
Half-cut cells
Many modern panels use cells cut in half, which reduces current per cell, lowers losses and improves shade tolerance.
Safety
DC strings carry high voltages whenever the sun shines and can't simply be "switched off" at the panels. Installation must follow strict rules.
Cells in series raise the voltage to something an inverter can use.

cards.title: Watt-peak
cards.text: Panels are rated in watt-peak (Wp): output under standard test conditions of 1,000 W/m² of sunlight at 25 °C. Real output is usually lower because of heat, angle and dust.

deep.x: Panels are rated in watt-peak (Wp): their output under standard test conditions (STC). Real-world output is usually lower.
Why real output is lower
Typical performance

v.unit: output of a 400 Wp panel, W (approx.)

deep.x: Price trends
Solar module prices fell by roughly 90% between 2010 and 2020 and kept falling in the 2020s, making solar one of the cheapest sources of new electricity.
Wp is a lab rating; real panels rarely hit it.

cards.title: How much will it produce?
cards.text: In Portugal, each kWp of well-oriented panels typically produces around 1,400–1,700 kWh a year, among the best in Europe.

deep.x: In Portugal, each kilowatt-peak of well-oriented panels produces roughly 1,400–1,700 kWh a year, one of the best yields in Europe.
Regional yields
Example
That's more than a typical Portuguese household uses in a year, though production and use don't match in time.
Seasons

items.b: up to twice the winter output

deep.x: Portugal's sun makes each solar panel worth about 60% more than in Germany.

cards.title: Orientation and tilt
cards.text: In Portugal, panels facing south at around 30–35° give the most energy over a year. East–west layouts produce less in total but spread production across the day.

deep.x: Panel orientation and tilt determine how much sunlight they capture over the year.
The optimum
In Portugal, south-facing panels tilted at roughly 30–35° collect the most energy over the year, close to the latitude minus a few degrees.
East–west layouts
Flat roofs
Panels on flat roofs are usually tilted on frames, or laid flatter in east–west rows to fit more panels on the roof.
South at 30–35° maximises energy; east–west better matches daily use.

cards.title: Shade matters
cards.text: A small shadow on one cell can cut a whole string's output, because cells in series carry the same current. Bypass diodes and optimisers limit the damage.

deep.x: Shading even a small part of a solar panel can reduce output disproportionately, because cells in series all carry the same current.
Bypass diodes
Panels contain bypass diodes, typically three per panel, that route current around shaded sections, limiting the loss to part of the panel.
Optimisers and microinverters

items: shade on one panel affects the string

deep.x: Hot spots
A shaded cell forced to carry current can heat up and be damaged. Persistent partial shading, such as from a chimney, should be avoided in design.
Check for chimneys, trees and antennas before deciding where panels go.

cards.title: Heat lowers output
cards.text: Silicon cells lose roughly 0.3–0.4% of output per °C above 25 °C. On a hot summer roof the cells can reach 60 °C, losing over 10%.

deep.x: Solar cells work better when cool. Silicon panels lose about 0.3–0.4% of output for every °C above 25 °C.
Example
Cooling helps

x: Mounting with air gaps behind panels

deep.x: Best months
In Portugal, spring often gives excellent output: strong sun, long days and cooler temperatures than midsummer.
Floating solar farms on reservoirs, such as Alqueva's, benefit from water cooling, which slightly improves efficiency.

cards.title: Self-consumption

items: Charge the EV in the sun
Add a battery for the evening

cards.text: Solar power is worth most when you use it as it's produced, because exported power earns less than imported power costs. Run the dishwasher, heat water or charge the car at midday.

deep.x: Solar power is most valuable when used directly at home, because exported electricity earns much less than imported electricity costs.
The economics
In Portugal
Household systems operate under the self-consumption regime (UPAC). Surplus can be sold to a supplier, and renewable energy communities let neighbours share solar.
Batteries
Use solar when the sun shines; export only what you can't.

cards.title: Inverters
cards.text: String inverters convert DC from the panels into AC for the home. Hybrid inverters can also charge and discharge a battery. Microinverters sit behind each panel.

deep.x: Inverters convert DC from panels into AC for the home and grid. They also optimise panel output and monitor performance.
Hybrid inverters
A hybrid inverter connects panels, a battery and the grid, deciding where energy goes moment by moment.
Maximum power point tracking
Lifespan
The inverter is the brain of a solar system, and often the first part to replace.

cards.title: Payback
cards.text: In sunny Portugal, a home system often pays for itself in roughly 5–8 years, depending on price, self-consumption and tariffs. Panels typically carry 25-year performance warranties.

deep.x: In Portugal's sunny climate, home solar systems often pay back their cost in roughly 5–8 years, then produce cheap electricity for decades.
What drives payback
Example
Degradation
Panels lose about 0.3–0.5% of output per year. After 25 years, good panels still produce more than 80% of their original output.
Sun, self-consumption and price decide how fast solar pays back.

quiz.q: What does "Wp" stand for?
options: Watt-peak, output under standard test conditions
quiz.explain: Rated at 1,000 W/m² and 25 °C.

quiz.q: Which direction should panels face in Portugal for maximum yearly energy?
quiz.explain: The sun crosses the southern sky.

quiz.q: Why do hot panels produce less?
options: Silicon cells lose efficiency as temperature rises
quiz.explain: About 0.35% per °C above 25 °C.

lessons.title: Choosing cables
lessons.summary: Cross-sections, voltage drop and why size matters.

cards.title: Cables heat up
cards.text: Every cable has some resistance, so current heats it (I² × R). Too small a cable for the current overheats, damages its insulation and can start a fire.

deep.x: Every cable has resistance, so current through it produces heat. Size the cable correctly and the heat is harmless; undersize it and insulation degrades or melts.
Doubling the current
What limits current
Insulation ratings
A cable's capacity is really its ability to get rid of heat.

cards.title: Cross-section in mm²
cards.text: Cable size is the copper area in square millimetres. Bigger area, lower resistance, more current it can safely carry.

deep.x: Cable size is given by the copper cross-sectional area in square millimetres. Larger area means lower resistance and more current capacity.
Resistance per metre
Diameter vs area
Area grows with the square of diameter: a 6 mm² conductor has four times the area of 1.5 mm², but only twice the diameter.
Not AWG
North America uses AWG gauge numbers, where bigger numbers mean thinner wires. Europe uses mm² directly.
Capacities depend on installation: always use the official tables.

cards.title: Typical sizes at home
cards.text: Common practice in Portugal: 1.5 mm² for lighting, 2.5 mm² for sockets, 4 mm² for ovens or water heaters, 6 mm² for an EV charger or big heat pump. Always check the installation rules and the installer's calculation.

deep.x: Typical residential practice in Portugal follows the RTIEBT technical rules. Sizes depend on load, length and installation method, so installers must calculate.
Supply cable
The cable from the meter to the board is sized for the contracted power, often 10 mm² or larger for single phase.
Long runs

x: 40 m run to a garden studio at 16 A

deep.x: Certification
New installations in Portugal require a project or declaration by a qualified electrician and inspection by an authorised body before connection.
Typical sizes are a starting point; the calculation decides.

cards.title: The breaker protects the cable

items.r: find the overload
rewire with thicker cable if needed

cards.text: The breaker must be rated so the cable can never carry more than it safely can. Swapping a 16 A breaker for a 25 A one "because it keeps tripping" removes the protection.

deep.x: A breaker's rating must never exceed what the cable can safely carry. Its job is to trip before the cable overheats.

items.w: Breaker keeps tripping, fit a bigger one
items.r: Find the cause: overload or fault

deep.x: Matching
Why upsizing is dangerous
Real causes of tripping

items: Too many appliances on one circuit

deep.x: If a breaker trips, it's doing its job: listen to it.

cards.title: Voltage drop
cards.text: Long cables lose voltage along the way. Rules usually limit the drop to a few percent. Single-phase drop is roughly twice the length times current times resistance per metre.

deep.x: Long cables lose voltage along their length. Too much drop makes motors struggle, lights dim and electronics misbehave.
Example
Limits
Fixes
For long runs, voltage drop often decides the cable size, not heat.

cards.title: Installation method matters
cards.text: A cable buried in insulation or bundled with others can't shed heat, so it carries less current safely than one in open air.

deep.x: How a cable is installed affects how well it sheds heat, and therefore how much current it can safely carry.

v.unit: relative capacity of the same cable, % (illustrative)

deep.x: Derating
Cable tables give base capacities, then correction factors for grouping, ambient temperature and thermal insulation.
Hot spots

x: Bundles of many circuits in one trunking
Cables near hot water pipes or in sunny areas

deep.x: Planning
The same cable can be safe in air and overheated in insulation.

cards.title: Colours
cards.text: In Europe: brown is live (phase), blue is neutral, green-and-yellow is protective earth. Older Portuguese installations may use different colours, so never trust colours alone.

deep.x: Conductor colours help identify their function. In Europe, harmonised colours have been standard for decades, but older installations may differ.
Never trust colours alone
Older or altered installations may use non-standard colours, and DIY work can swap them. Always test before touching.
Green-yellow is only for earth
The green-and-yellow conductor must never be used for anything other than protective earth.
Colours are a guide, not a guarantee.

cards.title: Flexible vs rigid
cards.text: Fixed wiring uses solid or stranded rigid conductors. Appliance leads and extension cords use flexible multi-strand cable that survives bending.

deep.x: Cables are built differently depending on whether they stay fixed or move.
Using the wrong one

x: Rigid cable in a moving application cracks over time
Flexible strands need ferrules in screw terminals to avoid loose strands

deep.x: Common types in Portugal
Outdoors
Outdoor cables need UV-resistant, waterproof sheaths, and buried cables need protection or armouring.
Fixed wiring stays rigid; anything that moves must be flexible.

cards.title: Extension leads

items: Check the max watts on the label

cards.text: A reel extension must be fully unrolled for high loads, otherwise the coiled cable traps heat and can melt. Never daisy-chain multi-plug adapters for heaters or kettles.

deep.x: Extension leads are convenient but often misused. Many electrical fires start with overloaded or damaged extensions.
Reels
A coiled reel traps heat; most have two ratings printed on them.
Multi-plug adapters
Plugging a heater, kettle and toaster into one adapter can exceed 16 A, overheating the adapter and the socket.
Warning signs
High-power appliances belong in wall sockets, not on extensions.

cards.title: Aluminium vs copper
cards.text: Aluminium conducts about 60% as well as copper, so it needs a bigger cross-section, but it's lighter and cheaper. Overhead power lines use aluminium; home wiring uses copper.

deep.x: Copper and aluminium are the main conductor metals. Each has its uses.
Weight advantage
For the same resistance, an aluminium conductor weighs about half as much as copper, which is why overhead lines use aluminium, often reinforced with a steel core.
Problems in homes
Aluminium wiring in some 1960s–70s homes in North America caused connection fires; special connectors are needed.
Today
Aluminium is widely used in large supply cables and distribution networks, with proper terminations.
Copper inside homes; aluminium on poles and pylons.

quiz.q: Which wire colour is protective earth in Europe?
quiz.explain: Brown live, blue neutral, green-yellow earth.

quiz.q: A 2.5 mm² socket circuit keeps tripping its 16 A breaker. What's right?
options: Find the overload or split the circuit
quiz.explain: The breaker protects the cable.

quiz.q: Why must a reel extension be unrolled for big loads?
options: Coiled cable can't shed heat and may melt
quiz.explain: The coil traps the heat.

lessons.title: Earthing and protection
lessons.summary: Breakers, RCDs, earth and surge protection.

cards.title: What earthing does
cards.text: Metal cases of appliances are connected to earth. If a live wire touches the case, current rushes to earth instead of through you, and a protective device trips.

deep.x: Earthing connects exposed metal parts of appliances and installations to the ground. If a fault makes them live, current flows to earth and protection trips, rather than through a person.
Without earthing
A live metal case would wait for someone to touch it. The person would become the path to earth.
Equipotential bonding
Bonding connects metal parts together so no dangerous voltage can appear between them.
Earthing systems

items.b: earth via a local electrode, common in Portuguese homes
combined neutral and earth in supply

deep.x: Earthing gives fault current a safe path that isn't you.

cards.title: The earth electrode
cards.text: In many homes the earth connection ends at a copper rod or ring buried in the ground. Its resistance must be low enough for protective devices to work, and it should be tested periodically.

deep.x: Many homes, including most in Portugal, connect to earth through a local electrode: a copper rod, plate or ring buried in the ground.
Resistance matters
With a 30 mA RCD, the limit is in theory up to about 1,600 Ω, but good practice aims far lower for reliability.
Soil affects it
Testing
Electricians measure earth resistance with special testers. It can change over time as soil dries or electrodes corrode.
In a TT system, the RCD does most of the protecting.

cards.title: Miniature circuit breakers
cards.text: An MCB trips two ways: a bimetallic strip for slow overloads (heat), and an electromagnet for short circuits (instant). The letter (B, C, D) sets how sensitive it is to inrush currents.

deep.x: A miniature circuit breaker (MCB) protects a circuit against overloads and short circuits. It has two tripping mechanisms.
Ratings
Why two mechanisms

x: A small, sustained overload heats the cable slowly, so a slow trip is fine
A short circuit needs instant disconnection

deep.x: Resettable
An MCB is a fuse you can reset.

cards.title: MCB curves

viz.unit: magnetic trip (× rated current, upper bound)

cards.text: Type B trips magnetically at 3–5× its rating, good for homes. Type C at 5–10×, for motors and lighting with big inrush. Type D at 10–20×, for heavy industrial motors.

deep.x: The curve letter sets how much current is needed to trip the breaker's magnetic mechanism instantly. It must suit the load's inrush current.

v.unit: instant trip threshold, multiples of rating

deep.x: Choosing
Inrush current
Motors, transformers and LED drivers draw a brief surge when switched on. A type B breaker may trip unnecessarily on large inrush loads.
Trade-off
Match the curve to what the circuit powers.

cards.title: RCD types

items: Type A: AC and pulsing DC

cards.text: Type AC detects only AC leakage. Type A also detects pulsing DC from electronics. Type B detects smooth DC too, often required for EV chargers and some solar inverters (or Type A with a DC-detection device).

deep.x: Residual current devices come in types that detect different kinds of leakage current. Modern electronics can produce leakage that older types can't see.
Where they're needed

items.b: washing machines, heat pumps with inverters

deep.x: EV chargers
Many EV chargers include a 6 mA DC detection device, allowing a Type A RCD upstream instead of a Type B.
Sensitivity
Electronics changed leakage currents; RCD types changed to match.

cards.title: RCBOs
cards.text: An RCBO combines an MCB and an RCD in one device, so a fault on one circuit only trips that circuit instead of the whole house.

deep.x: An RCBO combines an MCB and an RCD in one device, giving each circuit both overcurrent and leakage protection.

items: a fault trips only its own circuit

deep.x: Benefits

x: Fewer nuisance trips across the house
Fridge and freezer not affected by a fault elsewhere

deep.x: Cost
RCBOs cost more than separate devices, but are increasingly common in new installations.
Typical board
One circuit, one RCBO: faults stay local.

cards.title: Surge protection
cards.text: Lightning and grid switching can cause voltage spikes of thousands of volts for microseconds. A surge protection device (SPD) in the fuse board diverts them to earth, protecting electronics.

deep.x: Lightning strikes and grid switching can cause voltage spikes of thousands of volts lasting microseconds. Surge protection devices (SPDs) divert them to earth.
Types
What's at risk
SPDs wear out
Each surge consumes a little of the device's capacity. Many SPDs have indicator windows that change colour when they need replacing.
A small device in the board can save thousands of euros of electronics.

cards.title: Test your RCD
cards.text: RCDs have a test button that simulates a leak. Pressing it every few months checks that the mechanism isn't stuck. If it doesn't trip, call an electrician.

deep.x: RCDs have a test button that simulates a leakage current. Pressing it periodically checks the mechanism isn't stuck.
How often
Manufacturers commonly recommend testing every few months. It takes seconds.
What the button tests
Tip
Testing switches off the protected circuits, so reset clocks and check the fridge and freezer afterwards.
A stuck RCD gives no protection until you need it.

cards.title: Double insulation
cards.text: Some appliances have no earth wire: they're double insulated, shown by a square inside a square. Two layers of insulation protect you instead of an earth connection.

deep.x: Some appliances have no earth wire because they're double insulated (Class II). Two independent layers of insulation protect the user instead.

items.b: double insulated, two-core cable, square-in-square symbol

deep.x: Examples
The symbol
A square inside a square on the label means double insulation. It doesn't need an earth connection.
Damage
If the outer casing cracks, the double insulation is compromised. Damaged Class II appliances should be repaired or replaced.
No earth pin doesn't mean less safe, if it's double insulated.

cards.title: Fuses
cards.text: A fuse is a thin wire that melts when too much current flows. It works only once and must be replaced with the same rating. Old Portuguese installations may still have them; modern boards use breakers.

deep.x: A fuse is a thin conductor designed to melt when current exceeds its rating, breaking the circuit. It works once and must then be replaced.
Replacing correctly

items.w: Replace with a higher rating or wire
items.r: Replace with the same rating

deep.x: Types
Old installations
Older Portuguese homes may still have fuse boards and no RCD. Upgrading to modern breakers and RCDs is one of the most valuable electrical safety improvements.
If a fuse blows repeatedly, the fault is elsewhere.

quiz.q: Which RCD detects smooth DC leakage, as needed for many EV chargers?
quiz.explain: Type B covers smooth DC.

quiz.q: Why use RCBOs on each circuit?
options: A fault only trips that circuit
quiz.explain: Faults stay local.

quiz.q: What does an SPD protect against?
options: Short voltage spikes from lightning or switching
quiz.explain: It diverts surges to earth.

lessons.title: Three-phase power
lessons.summary: Why industry, big heat pumps and fast chargers use three wires.

cards.title: Three waves, offset
cards.text: Three-phase supply has three live conductors, each carrying an AC wave shifted by a third of a cycle (120°). At any moment at least one phase is near its peak, so power flows smoothly.

deep.x: Three-phase power uses three alternating voltages of the same frequency, each shifted by a third of a cycle (120°). Together they deliver power smoothly and efficiently.
Why smooth matters
Constant power means motors run smoothly with less vibration.
Balanced loads
When the three phases carry equal loads, their currents cancel in the neutral, which then carries almost nothing.
Invention
Polyphase AC systems were developed in the late 1880s by Nikola Tesla, Galileo Ferraris and Mikhail Dolivo-Dobrovolsky, who built the first three-phase transmission line in Germany in 1891.
Three overlapping waves deliver smooth, continuous power.

cards.title: 230 V and 400 V
cards.text: Between any phase and neutral you get 230 V; between two phases you get 400 V. Homes with three-phase supply still use 230 V for normal sockets.

deep.x: A three-phase supply provides two voltages: 230 V between any phase and neutral, and 400 V between any two phases.
Using both
Why √3?
Because the waves are 120° apart, the difference between two phases is √3 times the voltage of one phase, not double.
At home
Even in a three-phase home, normal sockets still provide 230 V. Only special outlets or appliances use 400 V.
230 V to neutral, 400 V between phases.

cards.title: Three-phase power
example: 16 A per phase at 400 V, cos φ = 1
cards.text: Three-phase carries about three times the power of a single phase with the same current per wire.

deep.x: Three-phase systems carry about three times the power of a single phase using the same current per conductor, with only modest extra copper.

v.f: P = √3 × V line × I × cos φ

deep.x: Examples
Comparison

v.unit: max power at 32 A per conductor, kW

deep.x: Copper efficiency
Same current per wire, three times the power.

cards.title: Why industry loves it
cards.text: Three-phase motors are simpler, smaller and self-starting, and transmission needs less copper for the same power. Nearly all generation, transmission and industrial loads are three-phase.

deep.x: Three-phase power is the standard for generation, transmission and industrial loads worldwide.
Motors
Three-phase currents create a rotating magnetic field naturally. Induction motors start and run without extra starting devices, and are smaller than single-phase motors of the same power.
Transmission
Why not more phases?
Six or twelve phases are possible, but three is the best compromise between smoothness and the number of conductors.
Three phases: the sweet spot of power engineering.

cards.title: Three-phase at home
cards.text: Larger homes in Portugal may have three-phase supply. It allows more contracted power, 11 kW or 22 kW EV charging, and big heat pumps, while circuits are spread across phases.

deep.x: Many Portuguese homes have single-phase supply, but larger homes and those with heavy loads can opt for three-phase.
When it makes sense
Costs

x: Installation changes and possibly a new meter
Fixed charges depend on contracted power, not the number of phases

deep.x: Distributing circuits
Circuits are spread across the three phases so each carries a similar load.
Some EVs can only charge at 7.4 kW on single phase but 11 kW on three-phase, cutting home charging time significantly.

cards.title: Balancing the phases
cards.text: Loads should be spread evenly across the three phases. If one phase carries most of the load, it may trip while the others are lightly used, and the neutral carries extra current.

deep.x: Loads should be spread evenly across the three phases. Unbalance wastes capacity and puts extra current on the neutral.
Problems with unbalance

x: One phase trips while others have spare capacity
Three-phase motors run hotter and less efficiently

deep.x: Planning
Harmonics
Some electronic loads produce harmonic currents that add up in the neutral instead of cancelling, so neutrals in office buildings may carry high currents even when phases are balanced.
Share the load and every phase does its fair part.

cards.title: Phase rotation

items.r: swap any two phases

cards.text: The order in which phases peak (L1, L2, L3) sets the direction a three-phase motor turns. Swap any two phases and the motor runs backwards: a classic commissioning check.

deep.x: The order in which the three phases peak (L1, L2, L3) is called phase rotation or sequence. It determines which way a three-phase motor spins.

items.r: Swap any two phases

deep.x: Why it matters
A pump running backwards may move little water and can be damaged; a conveyor may run the wrong way.
Checking
Electricians use a phase rotation tester before connecting motors.

steps: Connect tester to L1, L2, L3

deep.x: Swap two phases, reverse the motor.

cards.title: Star and delta
cards.text: Three-phase windings can be connected in star (Y), with a shared neutral point, or delta (Δ), in a triangle. Large motors often start in star to limit current, then switch to delta.

deep.x: Three-phase windings can be connected in two ways, each giving a different voltage across each winding.

items: one end of each winding joined
230 V per winding on 400 V supply

deep.x: Star-delta starting

steps: Start in star: lower voltage per winding

deep.x: Why reduce starting current
Large motors draw five to seven times their rated current when starting, causing voltage dips. Star-delta starters, soft starters and drives reduce this.
Transformers too
Distribution transformers often use delta on the high-voltage side and star on the low-voltage side, providing a neutral for 230 V loads.
Star to start gently, delta to run at full power.

cards.title: Grids are three-phase worldwide

steps: Houses spread across L1, L2, L3

cards.text: From the generator to the distribution transformer on your street, power travels as three-phase. Each house on a single-phase supply is connected to one of the three phases.

deep.x: From generator to street transformer, power travels as three-phase. Single-phase homes are connected to one of the three phases.
Spreading homes across phases
Distribution companies connect neighbouring homes to different phases to balance the load on each transformer.
Why your neighbour may have power
In a fault affecting one phase, some homes in a street lose power while neighbours on other phases don't.
Overhead lines
Your single phase is one third of a three-phase system.

cards.title: Spotting it

items: Three voltage readings on the meter
Brown, black and grey phase wires

cards.text: A three-phase board has three-pole or four-pole breakers and often a red CEE socket (5-pin) for machines. Three-phase meters show three readings.

deep.x: You can recognise a three-phase installation by its board, meter and outlets.
CEE sockets
Cables
Three-phase supply cables have five cores: three phases (brown, black, grey), neutral (blue) and earth (green-yellow).
Meter
A three-phase smart meter displays readings per phase and total.
Five-core cables and red sockets mean three-phase.

lessons.title: Power factor
lessons.summary: Real power, reactive power and why the grid cares.

cards.title: Real and apparent power
cards.text: With some loads, current and voltage don't peak at the same time. Then volts × amps (apparent power, in VA) is larger than the useful power that actually does work (real power, in W).

deep.x: When voltage and current don't rise and fall together, volts times amps (apparent power) exceeds the power doing useful work (real power).

v.f: Real power (W) = V × I × cos φ

deep.x: Example

x: With power factor 0.8: real power = 1,840 W

deep.x: What's happening
Why it costs
The extra current still flows through cables and transformers, causing losses and taking capacity, even though it does no useful work.
Power factor measures how usefully current is used.

cards.title: The beer analogy
cards.text: Picture a glass of beer: the liquid is real power that quenches thirst; the foam is reactive power that takes space but does no work. The whole glass is apparent power.

deep.x: A glass of beer helps visualise power factor: liquid, foam and the whole glass.
Reading the analogy

items.b: the foam: takes space, no work
the full glass: what the system must carry

deep.x: Less foam is better
A high power factor means mostly beer: the same glass delivers more useful power.
Where it falls short
Reactive power isn't truly wasted: it sustains magnetic fields that motors and transformers need. It just flows back and forth without being consumed.
Pay for the beer, but the glass must hold the foam too.

cards.title: What causes it
cards.text: Motors, transformers and fluorescent ballasts store energy in magnetic fields each cycle and give it back, so their current lags the voltage. Cheap electronics distort the current wave.

deep.x: Low power factor comes from loads that store energy in magnetic or electric fields, or that draw current in pulses.
Inductive loads
Coils store energy in magnetic fields during part of each cycle and release it later, so their current lags the voltage.
Electronics
Simple power supplies charge a capacitor only near the voltage peak, drawing short spikes of current. This distortion also lowers power factor.
Capacitive loads
Long underground cables and some LED drivers draw leading current, partly offsetting inductive loads.
Coils make current lag; cheap electronics make it spiky.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.text: A low power factor means more current for the same useful work: bigger cables, more losses, larger transformers. Utilities charge industrial customers for reactive energy.

deep.x: A low power factor means more current for the same useful work, increasing losses and requiring bigger equipment.

v.unit: current needed for 10 kW at 400 V three-phase, A

deep.x: Consequences
Utility charges
In Portugal, larger commercial and industrial customers are charged for reactive energy when their power factor falls below set thresholds, encouraging correction.
Grid perspective
Reactive power also affects voltage levels across the grid. Operators manage it carefully, and inverters at solar farms help regulate it.
Poor power factor makes everything carry more current than necessary.

cards.title: Correction with capacitors
cards.text: Capacitors draw current that leads the voltage, cancelling a motor's lagging current. Factories install capacitor banks to bring the power factor close to 1.

deep.x: Capacitors draw current that leads the voltage, cancelling the lagging current of motors. Factories install capacitor banks to keep the power factor close to 1.
Types of correction

items.b: switch capacitors in steps as load changes

deep.x: Typical target
Many installations aim for a power factor of 0.95 or above, avoiding penalties and freeing capacity.
Caution
Over-correction makes the power factor leading, which can cause overvoltage. Capacitors can also resonate with harmonics, so design matters.
Capacitors supply the reactive power locally so the grid doesn't have to.

cards.title: Units: W, VA, var
cards.text: Real power in watts (W), reactive power in volt-amperes reactive (var), apparent power in volt-amperes (VA). UPS units and generators are rated in VA because their wiring must handle the full current.

deep.x: Three related units describe the components of AC power.
Why VA ratings
UPS units, generators and transformers are rated in VA or kVA because their windings and electronics must handle the total current, whatever the power factor.
Generators
Generators are usually rated in kVA at a power factor of 0.8. A 10 kVA generator delivers about 8 kW of real power.
Watts do the work; VA sizes the equipment.

cards.title: The power triangle
cards.text: Real and reactive power are at right angles, so apparent power is the hypotenuse: VA² = W² + var². The angle between them is φ.

deep.x: Real power and reactive power are at right angles, like two sides of a right-angled triangle. Apparent power is the hypotenuse.
Example
Using it
Angle
The smaller the angle, the closer to 1 the power factor.

cards.title: Your home bill
cards.text: Households in Portugal pay for active energy (kWh) only; reactive energy charges apply to larger commercial and industrial customers. Your contracted power, though, is in kVA.

deep.x: Portuguese households pay only for active energy (kWh), not reactive energy. But contracted power is in kVA, which reflects current capacity.
Why kVA for contracted power
The limit protects cables and network capacity, which depend on current, not on how useful that current is. kVA captures current directly.
At home
Most household loads are resistive or have power factor correction, so kW and kVA are similar. Old motors and cheap electronics lower it slightly.
At home you pay for watts; your limit is in volt-amps.

cards.title: Power factor of devices
cards.text: Resistive loads like kettles and heaters have a power factor of 1. Motors run around 0.8–0.9 at full load and much lower when lightly loaded.

deep.x: Different appliances have very different power factors, depending on how they draw current.
Lightly loaded motors
A motor running at a fraction of its rated load still needs its magnetising current, so its power factor drops sharply. Oversized motors waste capacity.
Small electronics
Small LED bulbs and phone chargers often have low power factors, but their currents are tiny, so the impact is small.
Measuring
Plug-in energy monitors often display power factor, a fun way to explore appliances at home.
Resistive loads are perfect; motors and cheap electronics are not.

cards.title: PFC in chargers
cards.text: Larger electronic power supplies, including laptop and EV chargers, contain power factor correction circuits that make the current follow the voltage wave, as required by EU rules.

deep.x: Power factor correction (PFC) circuits make electronic power supplies draw current that follows the voltage wave smoothly, instead of in spikes.
Why required
EU rules on harmonic currents (standard EN 61000-3-2) set limits for equipment above about 75 W, effectively requiring PFC in larger power supplies.
Benefits
Active vs passive
Good chargers draw current as smoothly as a heater.

quiz.q: A load draws 1,000 VA with a power factor of 0.8. Its real power is…
quiz.explain: W = VA × cos φ = 800 W.

quiz.q: What corrects a lagging power factor in a factory?
quiz.explain: Capacitors cancel the lagging current.

quiz.q: Which device has a power factor of about 1?
quiz.explain: Pure resistance keeps current in step with voltage.

lessons.title: Using a multimeter
lessons.summary: Measuring volts, amps, ohms and continuity safely.

cards.title: One tool, many meters
cards.text: A multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance, and usually continuity, diodes and sometimes capacitance and temperature. A rotary dial chooses the function and range.

deep.x: A multimeter combines a voltmeter, ammeter and ohmmeter in one instrument, plus extra functions.
Parts
Digital vs analogue
Choosing one

x: Auto-ranging and True RMS for convenience and accuracy
CAT III 600 V or better for household use

deep.x: One instrument, many measurements: choose the function before touching anything.

cards.title: Measuring voltage
cards.text: Set the dial to V (AC ~ or DC ⎓), put the probes across the two points, in parallel. The meter has very high resistance, so it barely disturbs the circuit.

deep.x: Voltage is measured across a component or between two points, with the meter in parallel. The meter's high resistance means it barely affects the circuit.

steps: Choose V AC or V DC
Black lead to COM, red to V

deep.x: AC or DC
Typical readings
Safety

x: Hold probes by the insulated grips, fingers behind the guards
Connect black first, red second; remove red first
Never measure voltage with leads in the current socket

deep.x: Voltage is measured across, in parallel.

cards.title: Measuring current

items: red lead in A or mA

cards.text: Current must flow through the meter, in series: break the circuit and insert the meter. Move the red lead to the A or mA socket. Forgetting to move it back is the classic way to blow the meter's fuse.

deep.x: Current must flow through the meter: you break the circuit and insert the meter in series.
Steps

steps: Move red lead to A or mA

deep.x: The classic mistake
Leaving the red lead in the A socket and then measuring voltage creates a near short circuit through the meter, blowing its fuse or worse.

items.w: Measure voltage with lead in A socket
items.r: Always return red lead to V socket

deep.x: Easier options
For mains currents, a clamp meter is safer and faster. For small electronics, the mA range is fine.
Current goes through the meter, so the circuit must be opened.

cards.title: Resistance and continuity
cards.text: Measure resistance only on unpowered circuits. Continuity mode beeps when the resistance is very low: perfect for finding broken wires or checking which cable is which.

deep.x: Resistance and continuity measurements use the meter's own small battery, so the circuit must be unpowered.
Uses

items.b: find broken wires, check fuses, identify cables

deep.x: Example
Why unpowered
Measuring resistance on a live circuit gives wrong readings and can damage the meter.
Continuity mode is the fastest way to find a broken wire.

cards.title: CAT ratings

items: CAT IV: supply origin, meter tails
CAT III: fuse boards, fixed wiring

cards.text: Meters carry a category rating for where they're safe to use. CAT II covers plugged-in appliances, CAT III the fixed installation and fuse boards, CAT IV the supply origin. Use at least CAT III 600 V on house wiring.

deep.x: Measurement categories (CAT) indicate where a meter can safely be used. The closer to the supply origin, the higher the possible energy of transients.

items: CAT IV: supply origin, meters, service cable
CAT III: fixed installation, distribution boards

deep.x: Why it matters
A high-energy voltage spike on a fuse board can make a poorly rated meter fail violently. CAT ratings guarantee the meter's insulation and protection can handle it.
Recommendation
Leads count too
Test leads have their own CAT ratings. The system rating is the lowest of meter and leads.
A cheap meter on a fuse board is a hazard, not a bargain.

cards.title: Clamp meters

items.r: clamp a single conductor
separate live from neutral

cards.text: A clamp meter measures current without breaking the circuit: you clamp it around a single conductor and it reads the magnetic field. Clamp around the whole cable and live and neutral cancel out.

deep.x: A clamp meter measures current by sensing the magnetic field around a conductor, without breaking the circuit.

items.r: Clamp around one conductor only

deep.x: Why only one conductor
Live and neutral carry equal currents in opposite directions. Clamp both and their fields cancel, reading zero.
Uses
Leakage clamps
Sensitive clamp meters can measure milliamp leakage by clamping both live and neutral: any reading is current escaping to earth, useful for finding nuisance RCD trips.
AC and DC
Basic clamp meters measure only AC. DC clamps use Hall-effect sensors, useful for solar and battery systems.
Clamp one wire to measure current safely and quickly.

cards.title: Auto-range and True RMS
cards.text: Auto-ranging meters pick the range for you. True RMS meters measure non-sinusoidal waveforms (from inverters, LED drivers, VFDs) correctly; cheaper meters can be quite wrong on these.

deep.x: Two features that make a multimeter more convenient and more accurate.
True RMS

items: accurate only for pure sine waves

deep.x: Why it matters today
Modern electrical systems are full of distorted waveforms from inverters, LED drivers, variable speed drives and chargers. Average-responding meters can be off by 30% or more on such signals.
When it doesn't matter
For DC measurements and resistive loads on clean mains, any decent meter is accurate.
For modern electronics and inverters, True RMS is worth paying for.

cards.title: Checking a socket
cards.text: To check a socket is live, measure between live and neutral (about 230 V), live and earth (about 230 V) and neutral and earth (near 0 V). Proper socket testers also check earth and RCD.

deep.x: A multimeter can check that a socket is live and correctly wired, though dedicated socket testers check more.
What readings mean
Socket testers
Plug-in testers show wiring faults with lights, and some can trigger the RCD to check it trips. They're cheaper and faster for routine checks.
Safety
Use proper probes with shrouded tips, CAT-rated, and never insert probes in a damaged socket.
Three measurements tell you if a socket is healthy.

cards.title: Prove dead before you touch

steps: Test tester on a live source

cards.text: Before working on any circuit: isolate it, lock it off, test it's dead with a proven tester, and re-check the tester on a known live source. Never trust a switch or a label alone.

deep.x: The most important electrical safety procedure: prove a circuit is dead before working on it. Never trust switches, labels or assumptions.
Why test the tester
A broken tester reads "0 V" on a live circuit. Checking it on a known live source before and after proves it was working.
Common traps
Voltage indicators
If you haven't tested it, assume it's live.

cards.title: Reading batteries and sensors
cards.text: Multimeters are great for electronics: battery health (a "12 V" battery should read about 12.6 V when full), sensor outputs, and checking a 3.3 V rail on an ESP32 board.

deep.x: Multimeters are invaluable for electronics and battery checks.

v.unit: 12 V lead-acid resting voltage vs charge

deep.x: Other batteries
Electronics

x: Check a 3.3 V rail on an ESP32 or Arduino board
Read sensor outputs, such as 0–10 V or 4–20 mA signals

deep.x: Load matters
A weak battery can show normal voltage with no load but collapse under load. Testing under load gives a truer picture.
Resting voltage is a quick health check; load testing tells the full story.

lessons.title: Charging electric cars
lessons.summary: AC, DC, kW and why charging slows down.

cards.title: AC charging
cards.text: At home and on most street posts, the car receives AC and converts it to DC with its own on-board charger. The car's charger limits the speed, usually 7–11 kW.

deep.x: With AC charging, the car receives alternating current and converts it to DC with its own on-board charger. Most home and street charging is AC.

steps: Car's on-board charger converts to DC

deep.x: Limits
Charging speed is the lowest of
Typical time
For AC, the car's own charger sets the speed.

cards.title: DC fast charging
cards.text: Fast chargers convert AC to DC in the station and feed the battery directly, bypassing the car's charger. Powers range from 50 kW to 350 kW.

deep.x: DC fast chargers convert AC to DC inside the station and feed the battery directly, bypassing the car's on-board charger.
Power levels
Cost
DC fast charging is usually more expensive per kWh than home charging, reflecting the costly equipment and grid connections.
Battery health
Frequent fast charging adds some stress, but modern battery management limits power when the battery is cold or nearly full. Real-world data show modest effects for typical use.
DC is for journeys; AC is for daily life.

cards.title: Charging power options
cards.text: A normal socket gives about 2.3 kW (10 A at 230 V), slow but fine overnight for short commutes. A single-phase wallbox at 32 A gives about 7.4 kW.

deep.x: Charging speed depends on the power available. Even slow charging covers most daily driving overnight.
Range added per hour
Domestic sockets
A normal Schuko socket can charge slowly, but long sessions at 10 A heat sockets and plugs. A dedicated circuit or wallbox is safer for regular use.
Most people need only a modest home charger.

cards.title: How long will it take?
cards.text: Divide the energy needed by the charging power, then add some margin for losses and the slower final stage.

deep.x: Estimating charging time is simple arithmetic, with a margin for losses and the slower final stage.
Examples
Daily needs
Practical tip
Most EV owners don't charge from empty to full. They plug in at night and top up what they used that day.
Daily driving usually needs only an hour or two of home charging.

cards.title: The charging curve
cards.text: DC charging is fastest at low states of charge and slows down as the battery fills, to protect it. Going from 10% to 80% often takes about as long as 80% to 100%.

deep.x: DC charging power isn't constant. It's highest at low charge and tapers as the battery fills, to protect the cells.
Why it tapers
As the battery fills, cell voltage rises close to its limit. The BMS reduces current to avoid stressing the cells and causing lithium plating.
Road trip strategy

items.b: the last 20% takes as long as the first 70%

deep.x: Temperature
Cold batteries charge slowly. Many EVs pre-condition the battery when you navigate to a fast charger, warming it for faster charging.
On trips, charge 10–80% often rather than to 100%.

cards.title: 400 V and 800 V cars
cards.text: Most EVs use about 400 V packs. Some newer cars, such as the XPeng G9 and Porsche Taycan, use 800 V platforms, which allow higher charging power with less current and heat.

deep.x: Most EVs use battery packs of around 400 V. Some newer models use 800 V architectures for faster charging and lighter wiring.
Benefits of 800 V
Examples

items.b: Porsche Taycan, Hyundai Ioniq 5, Kia EV6, Audi e-tron GT

deep.x: Compatibility
800 V cars can use 400 V chargers through internal converters or by switching battery halves, sometimes at reduced power.
Higher voltage lets the same cable carry more power.

cards.title: Connectors in Europe
cards.text: Type 2 is the standard AC plug in Europe. CCS2 adds two big DC pins below it for fast charging. Older Japanese cars may use CHAdeMO.

deep.x: Europe has standardised EV connectors, which makes charging simpler than in some other regions.

items.b: Type 2 plus two DC pins, fast charging

deep.x: EU rules
EU law requires public AC chargers to provide Type 2 and DC fast chargers to provide CCS2, ensuring compatibility across countries.
Tesla in Europe
Tesla cars sold in Europe use CCS2, and many Tesla Superchargers in Europe are open to other brands.
Cables
In Europe, Type 2 and CCS2 cover almost every car and charger.

cards.title: Smart charging at home
cards.text: Smart wallboxes can follow cheaper night tariffs, use surplus solar, and reduce power if the house is near its contracted limit (load balancing), so the main breaker doesn't trip.

deep.x: Smart wallboxes adjust charging to prices, solar production and household load, saving money and avoiding tripping the main breaker.
Load balancing

steps: Wallbox reduces charging when oven is on

deep.x: Solar charging
In solar mode, the wallbox charges only with surplus solar power. Most cars need at least about 1.4 kW (6 A) to charge, so there must be enough surplus.
Requirements in Portugal

A wallbox should be installed on a dedicated circuit with appropriate RCD protection by a certified installer. Condominium rules allow residents to install chargers in their parking spaces under specific procedures.
Smart charging uses cheap, clean hours without tripping the house.

cards.title: Mobi.E in Portugal

steps: Choose a supplier card or app
Plug in at any Mobi.E point

cards.text: Portugal's public charging network is coordinated by Mobi.E. You can use most public chargers with one card or app from any supplier (CEME), and pay the operator, the supplier and network fees.

deep.x: Portugal's public charging network is coordinated by Mobi.E, which manages the platform that connects charging operators, electricity suppliers for mobility and users.
The players
What you pay
Changing rules
EU rules (AFIR) now require new fast chargers to accept card payments directly, and Portugal has been reforming its charging model to make ad-hoc payment simpler.
Mobi.E was launched in 2010, making Portugal one of the first countries with a nationwide interoperable charging network.

cards.title: Efficiency and losses
cards.text: Some energy is lost as heat while charging, typically about 10% for AC home charging, sometimes more at very low power. The meter at the wallbox shows more kWh than the battery receives.

deep.x: Not all energy from the grid reaches the battery. Some is lost as heat in the charger, cables and battery.
Why low power is less efficient
The car's electronics, pumps and battery management run during charging. At low power, these fixed losses form a larger share.
What it means
Reducing losses
Pay for the kWh at the plug, not only what reaches the battery.

quiz.explain: AC charging uses the car's own charger.

lessons.title: Energy at home
lessons.summary: Bills, tariffs and where the kWh go.

cards.title: Reading the bill
cards.text: A Portuguese electricity bill has a fixed part (contracted power, per day), an energy part (per kWh), network access charges, taxes (VAT, the audiovisual contribution) and sometimes discounts.

deep.x: A Portuguese electricity bill has several components. Understanding them helps choose the right tariff and contracted power.

items: Fixed charge: contracted power per day

deep.x: Typical breakdown
Taxes

items.b: reduced rate on part of consumption for smaller contracts, 23% on the rest
audiovisual contribution, a few euros a month
small special consumption tax per kWh

deep.x: Social tariff
Low-income households can receive the "tarifa social", a significant automatic discount on electricity.
Look at both the kWh price and the fixed daily charge when comparing offers.

cards.title: Time-of-use tariffs

items: worth it if you shift load

cards.text: Simple tariffs charge the same price all day. Two-period (bi-horário) tariffs have cheaper off-peak (vazio) hours, mostly at night and weekends; three-period (tri-horário) splits peak and shoulder hours too.

deep.x: Time-of-use tariffs charge different prices at different times of day. Cheaper off-peak hours reward shifting consumption.

items: cheaper off-peak (vazio), mostly at night and weekends

deep.x: Daily vs weekly cycles

items.b: off-peak hours at the same times every day

deep.x: Typical off-peak window
In the daily cycle, off-peak typically runs overnight (for example 22:00–08:00). Exact times depend on the cycle and season.
Dynamic tariffs
Some suppliers offer prices that follow the wholesale market hour by hour (indexed tariffs), which can be very cheap at midday on sunny days or at night.
The best tariff depends on when you use electricity.

cards.title: When bi-horário pays off
cards.text: It usually pays if you can move a good share of your consumption, often around 40% or more, to off-peak hours: EV charging, water heating, washing machine and dishwasher on a timer.

deep.x: Bi-horário tariffs have cheaper off-peak prices but more expensive peak prices than simple tariffs. They pay off only if you shift enough consumption.
Break-even
Calculate
Simulators
ERSE, the Portuguese energy regulator, provides an online simulator to compare tariffs and suppliers.
Shift heavy, flexible loads to night and bi-horário can save real money.

cards.title: Where the kWh go
cards.text: In a typical home, heating and hot water are the biggest users, followed by cooking, refrigeration, laundry and lighting. An EV can easily double household consumption.

deep.x: Household electricity use depends on whether heating and hot water are electric, and on appliances and habits.
An EV changes everything

x: similar to a typical home's total consumption

deep.x: Where savings are biggest
Measure first
A plug-in energy monitor or smart meter data reveals your real big users.

cards.title: The fridge runs all year

cards.title: Static charge
cards.text: Rubbing two materials together transfers electrons from one to the other. One becomes negatively charged, the other positively. The charge stays put ("static") until it finds a path.

deep.x: Static electricity is charge that builds up on a surface and stays there. Rubbing materials together transfers electrons from one to the other.

steps: Electrons move from one to the other

deep.x: The triboelectric series
Everyday examples
Why dry weather
Humid air helps charge leak away. In dry winter air or air-conditioned buildings, charge builds up more easily.
Static is electricity standing still, waiting to jump.

cards.title: Why you get shocks
cards.text: Walking on carpet in dry weather builds up charge on your body, sometimes thousands of volts. Touch a metal door handle and it discharges in a tiny spark. Harmless to you, but deadly for electronics.

items.l: roughly where you start to feel a spark

items: Touch metal with a key first

Sensitivity

Keep components in their bags until needed
Avoid working on carpet in dry weather

Thunder distance

x: Count seconds between flash and thunder

Scale

x: They don't attract lightning from far away

items.r: The metal body carries current around the occupants

Current flows over the outer metal surface and jumps to the ground. The inside stays largely protected.

cards.title: Three dangers
cards.text: Electricity hurts in three ways: electric shock (current through the body), burns (from arcs or hot surfaces) and fire (from overheating cables or connections).

Fire
Protection

cards.title: Current path matters
cards.text: Current from hand to hand or hand to foot crosses the chest and heart, the most dangerous paths. Wet skin has much lower resistance, letting more current flow at the same voltage.

Wet skin
Water dramatically lowers skin resistance, so the same voltage drives much more current.

Even moderate currents become dangerous when they last longer. Fast disconnection by RCDs is crucial.

cards.text: Home batteries don't always pay for themselves on savings alone. The case improves with large evening consumption, time-of-use tariffs, low feed-in prices, or a strong need for backup.

deep.x: Home batteries don't always pay for themselves through savings alone. The business case depends on how they're used.
A simple estimate

x: 7 kWh battery cycling 300 days a year

deep.x: With a battery costing several thousand euros, simple payback can exceed ten years.
What improves the case
Batteries often make more sense for resilience than for pure savings.

cards.title: Safety and placement
cards.text: Install batteries in a ventilated, cool, dry place, away from bedrooms and exits, with clearances as the manufacturer specifies. LFP chemistry is preferred for homes because it's more thermally stable.

deep.x: Home batteries store a lot of energy. Proper placement and installation reduce fire risk and extend battery life.

Certification
Choose batteries certified to recognised safety standards and installed by qualified installers, with proper protection and isolation.
A well-placed LFP battery is a safe neighbour.

lessons.title: A history of electricity
lessons.summary: From amber to the smart grid.

cards.title: Amber and the word "electric"
cards.text: Ancient Greeks noticed that rubbed amber attracted feathers. The Greek word for amber, "elektron", gave us "electricity", a term coined by William Gilbert around 1600.

deep.x: Electricity's name comes from amber. Ancient Greeks noticed that rubbed amber attracted light objects like feathers and straw.
Gilbert's work
English physician William Gilbert's 1600 book "De Magnete" studied magnetism and static electricity, coining the Latin word "electricus" (amber-like) for materials that attract when rubbed.
Elektron

items.b: first used in English by Thomas Browne, 1646

deep.x: Early experiments
Electricity is named after a fossilised tree resin.

cards.title: Volta's battery, 1800
cards.text: Alessandro Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked cloth: the first battery to give a steady current. The volt is named after him.

deep.x: Alessandro Volta's "voltaic pile" was the first source of steady electric current, opening the door to modern electrical science.
The frog debate
Luigi Galvani had observed frog legs twitching with metals and believed in "animal electricity". Volta argued the metals generated the electricity and built the pile to prove it.
Consequences
Humphry Davy used powerful batteries to isolate sodium and potassium in 1807.
Honour
The volt is named after Volta. Napoleon made him a count in recognition of his work.
The battery turned electricity from sparks into a steady flow.

cards.title: Faraday's discoveries
cards.text: In 1831 Michael Faraday showed that moving magnets induce currents, the basis of every generator and transformer. He had little formal education and became one of the greatest experimenters ever.

deep.x: Michael Faraday, largely self-taught, made some of the most important discoveries in electrical science.

items.l: born to a blacksmith's family in London

deep.x: From apprentice to scientist
Faraday left school early and became a bookbinder's apprentice, reading the books he bound. He attended Humphry Davy's lectures and became his assistant at the Royal Institution.
His legacy
The farad
The unit of capacitance, the farad, honours him.
Faraday started the Royal Institution's Christmas Lectures for young people in 1825; they continue today.

cards.title: Maxwell's equations
cards.text: In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell wrote four equations unifying electricity, magnetism and light. They predicted radio waves, which Hertz demonstrated in 1887.

deep.x: In the 1860s, James Clerk Maxwell described electricity, magnetism and light in one theory. It remains one of the greatest achievements in physics.
The prediction
Maxwell's equations showed that changing electric and magnetic fields create waves travelling at the speed of light, so light itself must be an electromagnetic wave.
The four equations in words

items.b: magnetic field lines have no start or end
changing magnetic fields create electric fields
currents and changing electric fields create magnetic fields

deep.x: Impact
Maxwell revealed that light is electricity and magnetism dancing together.

cards.title: Light bulbs

events.l: homes widely electrified in the US

cards.text: Many inventors worked on electric light. In 1879 Edison and, in Britain, Swan produced practical long-lasting carbon-filament bulbs. Edison also built the power stations and network to sell electricity.

deep.x: Electric light transformed daily life. Many inventors contributed, but Edison and Swan produced the first practical long-lasting bulbs around 1879.
Edison's system
Edison's genius was not only the bulb but the whole system: generators, wiring, meters and fuses. His Pearl Street station in New York opened in 1882.
Ediswan
After a patent dispute in Britain, Edison and Swan merged their British companies in 1883 as "Ediswan".
From filaments to LEDs
Nobel Prize
Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura received the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics for blue LEDs, which made white LED lighting possible.
The light bulb needed a whole electrical system to shine.

cards.title: Electricity in Portugal
cards.text: The first electric lights in Portugal were switched on in Cascais in 1878. Large hydroelectric dams from the 1950s onward, on rivers such as the Zêzere and the Douro, powered the country's electrification.

deep.x: Electricity reached Portugal in the late 19th century, and hydropower drove electrification across the 20th century.

events.l: Central Tejo power station in Lisbon

deep.x: Central Tejo
Lisbon's Central Tejo power station, built in stages from 1909, supplied much of the city's electricity until the 1970s. It's now part of the MAAT museum in Belém.
Hydro era

items: Castelo do Bode on the Zêzere

deep.x: No nuclear
Portugal never built a nuclear power plant. A project at Ferrel, near Peniche, was abandoned in the 1970s after local protests.
Modern era
Portugal electrified with water, then wind and sun.

cards.title: The transistor, 1947
cards.text: At Bell Labs, Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley built the first transistor. It replaced bulky vacuum tubes and made modern electronics, computers and phones possible.

deep.x: The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in December 1947, is the foundation of all modern electronics.
The inventors
John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for the transistor.
Scale
What a transistor does

items.b: small signal controls a larger one

deep.x: Billions of tiny switches now fit on a fingernail-sized chip.

cards.title: Nuclear and renewables
cards.text: The first nuclear power plants appeared in the 1950s. From the 2000s, wind and then solar grew rapidly as costs fell; solar module prices dropped by around 90% in the 2010s.

deep.x: The second half of the 20th century brought nuclear power; the 21st brought the rapid rise of wind and solar.
Falling costs
Nuclear today
Nuclear provides around a tenth of the world's electricity, with low carbon emissions but high construction costs and long build times.
Renewables today
Wind and solar are now the cheapest sources of new electricity in many countries, and their share grows every year.
Renewables went from expensive niche to cheapest option in about a decade.

cards.title: Units named after people
cards.text: Many units honour scientists: volt (Volta), ampere (Ampère), ohm (Ohm), watt (Watt), hertz (Hertz), coulomb (Coulomb), tesla (Tesla).

deep.x: Most electrical units honour scientists who made key discoveries.
More units
Writing rules

items.r: 230 volts (230 V), 10 amps (10 A)

deep.x: Unit names are lowercase when written out; symbols for units named after people are capitalised.
James Watt worked on steam engines, not electricity, but his name became the universal unit of power.

cards.title: What's next
cards.text: Electricity is taking over more of energy use: cars, heating, industry. The challenges now are storage, grid expansion, and matching variable renewable supply with demand.

deep.x: Electricity is taking over more of the energy system. The challenges now are storage, grids and flexibility.
Electrification

items.l: electricity's share of global final energy
as cars, heating and industry electrify

deep.x: Challenges
Data centres and AI
Rapid growth of data centres, driven partly by AI, is increasing electricity demand in several countries, including new projects in Portugal such as at Sines.
The future of energy is increasingly electric.
